lines.speaker: Terpsion
lines.text: Tell me, Pluto — is this fair? I'm dead at thirty, and Thoucritusm that old wreck, is still up there past ninety?
lines.note: Terpsion opens indignant, not philosophical. The outrage is sincere and therefore immediately funny.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: Perfectly fair, actually. He lives without praying for any of his friends to die. You spent the entire time plotting against him and waiting for the inheritance.
lines.note: Pluto delivers this as a simple statement of the file in front of him. No heat, no sarcasm — just the record.

lines.speaker: Terpsion
lines.text: Shouldn't an old man who can't even enjoy his wealth anymore step aside and make room for the young?
lines.note: Terpsion shifts to the philosophical register — still totally self-interested, but now dressed up as principle.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: Interesting legislation. 'Anyone too old to enjoy their money shall be required to die.' Fate and Nature arranged things differently, I'm afraid.
lines.note: 'Interesting legislation' — dry, not contemptuous. Pluto has heard worse.

lines.speaker: Terpsion
lines.text: Then I blame Fate and Nature. Things ought to go in order — the older one first, then the next oldest, then the one after that. No reversals. None of this business where some ancient wreck with three teeth left, barely able to see, draped over four servants, nose running, eyes crusted shut, no idea what pleasure is anymore — a living tomb that the young mock behind his back — none of this business where he gets to stay while the finest, strongest young men are the ones who die. That's rivers flowing uphill. At the very least, we should have been able to know in advance when each old man was going to go, so we wouldn't waste our time on the wrong ones. As it is — well, the proverb says it: the cart often carries the ox.
lines.note: Terpsion's long complaint is sitcom ranting dressed as philosophy. The list of the old man's indignities ('three teeth left, nose running') is increasingly vivid — he has clearly rehearsed this. Deadpan delivery throughout; the comedy is in the specificity.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: All of that is actually a great deal more sensible than you think it is. [pause] But let me ask you something. What on earth possesses people like you to drool over other men's property and attach yourselves to childless old men? The result is that you get buried before them and everyone finds it absolutely delightful. The harder you pray for them to die, the more everyone enjoys watching you go first. You've invented a remarkable new kind of love affair: you fall passionately in love with old women and old men — especially the childless ones. The ones with children leave you completely cold. And of course, plenty of your beloved targets have worked out exactly what you're up to, and even when they do have children, they pretend to hate them — so they can have admirers too. Then the will is read, and all the long-suffering courtiers are locked out, and the child and blood-inheritance win, exactly as they should, and the flatterers are left grinding their teeth.
lines.note: Pluto shifts to a lecture, but it's a satisfied lecture — he's enjoying this. The speech is long but it builds: from 'sensible' to the trap-mechanism of the scheme to the final image of the flatterers grinding their teeth. Slight warmth at 'the child and blood-inheritance win, exactly as they should' — he approves.

lines.speaker: Terpsion
lines.text: You're not wrong. Do you know how much Throucitus extracted from me? Always seeming like he was about to die — whenever I walked in he'd be moaning, making this tiny, half-formed sound from somewhere deep in his chest, like a chick that hasn't quite made it out of the egg. I was convinced he'd be in his coffin any minute, so I kept sending extravagant gifts — couldn't let the other suitors outspend me — and most nights I lay awake running the numbers, working out the arrangements. That's what killed me, as it turns out. Insomnia and anxiety. And him? He swallowed every scrap of bait I threw him, and was standing right there at my funeral a few days ago. [pause] Laughing.
lines.note: The chick-that-hasn't-made-it-out-of-the-egg simile is Terpsion's one moment of genuine literary invention. Let it land before 'I was convinced.' The final single word 'Laughing' should be a beat on its own — the pause before it is the punchline mechanism.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: Well done, Thoucriturus. Long may you live — wealthy, and laughing at men like this. May you not die until you've sent every last one of your flatterers on ahead.
lines.note: Pluto addresses the absent Thoucriturus directly — a brief, genuine endorsement. The comedy is that he is sincerely rooting for the old man.

lines.speaker: Terpsion
lines.text: Actually, [pause] that would be quite satisfying to me too — if Charoiades goes before Throucitus as well.
lines.note: Terpsion can't help himself. Even now, he's rooting against his rivals.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: Don't worry. Pheidon, Melanthos — all of them, the whole lot — they'll be along before him. Same cause of death.
lines.note: Pluto rattles off the names with the brisk assurance of someone checking a list. No drama needed.

lines.speaker: Terpsion
lines.text: I approve of that entirely. [beat] Long life to you, Thoucriturus.
lines.note: The closing line lands as the episode's ironic button: Terpsion, the dead man who prayed for the old man's death his whole life, is now sincerely wishing him a long one — because it means his rivals suffer first. Deadpan throughout.
